title.en: Identify semantic, psychological, organisational and personal barriers

say.en: An engineer explains a delay to the sales team using technical terms; the sales head, already annoyed, half-listens; the message passes through two more levels. By the time it reaches customers, it is wrong. In this lesson: Identify semantic, psychological, organisational and personal barriers.
Explain each with examples.
Suggest ways to improve communication.

body.en: Semantic *barriers* arise from words and symbols: badly expressed messages, words with several meanings, faulty translation, technical jargon and unclarified assumptions. Psychological barriers arise from the state of mind: premature evaluation, lack of attention, loss in transmission, distrust and emotions. Organisational barriers arise from the structure: rigid rules, too many levels, status differences and poor facilities. Personal barriers arise from individuals: a superior's fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence in subordinates, lack of time, and an employee's unwillingness to communicate or lack of incentive.

points.en: Personal: attitudes of superiors and subordinates

body.en: Clarify ideas before communicating; use simple language suited to the receiver; consult others when planning *communication*; mind the tone and body language; convey things of help and value to the listener; ask for feedback; follow up; and be a good listener. Organisations can also shorten chains of command, keep an open-door policy, use several channels and train staff in communication.

problem.en: A company finds that only half of its policy messages are understood on the shop floor. Messages pass through 4 levels, each losing about 15%. It plans to cut to 2 levels and require feedback at each step, which cuts the loss per step to about 5%. Estimate the improvement.

steps.en: Fewer levels (an organisational remedy) and feedback (a general remedy) work together.

answer.en: Understanding rises from about 52% to about 90%.

say.en: Let us work this out step by step. A company finds that only half of its policy messages are understood on the shop floor. Messages pass through 4 levels, each losing about 15 percent. It plans to cut to 2 levels and require feedback at each step, which cuts the loss per step to about 5 percent. Estimate the improvement.
Now: 0.85 to the power 4 is approximately 0.52, about 52 percent understood.
After the change: 0.95 squared is approximately 0.90, about 90 percent understood.
Fewer levels an organisational remedy and feedback a general remedy work together.
So the answer is Understanding rises from about 52 percent to about 90 percent.
